rationale: A wins because it respects the fact boundary better. Its category angle says, "not proof it's already an industry-wide move, since no other vendor's language is in evidence here," which is exactly the restraint a founder needs before emailing a reporter. B has the sharper package, but "The spreadsheet-database is trying to become an agent platform — in a category that already has incumbents" smuggles in a competitive premise the update did not supply.
gaps_in_A: "employees are the ones left to catch what they get wrong" asserts an employee burden and lack of safeguards that are not in the update.
"send communications" drifts past the supplied fact that agents draft emails; drafting is not sending.
The future-of-work angle partly duplicates the reliability angle. It has a different protagonist, but without employee proof it is a dressed-up workplace take.
"All four angles are blocked on the same gaps" muddles proof priorities; the valuation, category, reliability, and customer-story gaps are not the same gap.
gaps_in_B: "in a category that already has incumbents" and "late to a crowded category" invent a competitive premise. No competitor facts were supplied.
"down-round dynamics" overstates the valuation fact. The update says $11B is below a higher peak, not that there was a down round.
"bad draft sent" slides from drafting emails into sending them. That is exactly the kind of tiny overclaim that gets punished in a reporter's inbox.
"Draft one tight pitch" comes too early. The strongest angle still needs an on-record reliability or guardrail answer before it should become a pitch.
